chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter takes place on Susie and Sunitha's coconut farm in Kerala. Arrays of coconuts, bags, crates, oil, husk and a market stall carry every division, from the two division facts of one multiplication fact to dividing thousands by a two-digit number with a remainder. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.title: Videos teach, tools explore
points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student explores, builds and checks the idea alone, with hints, retry and reset. Eight tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own plan.

points.title: A tool in three steps
points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own question, used exactly as the book gives it.

points.title: Every book question has its own video
points.text: Every solved example, Let Us Do and Let Us Solve question and every answerable prompt of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.

points.title: Two ways to divide, side by side
points.text: Susie takes away many small groups and Sunitha takes away the biggest groups that fit. The chapter also divides by place value. The student sees that every method gives the same quotient and the same remainder, and checks each answer with N = D × Q + R.

points.title: Only the book's numbers
points.text: Every number on the farm, in a bill or in a word problem is the book's own. Any number the plan adds to teach an idea is a practice value and is said to be one.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Susie and Sunitha lay their coconuts out in 5 rows with 7 coconuts in each row. How many coconuts is that, and in how many ways can you split them into equal groups?
2. Susie and Sunitha have a large coconut farm in Kerala. Today they lay coconuts out in an array: 5 rows, and 7 coconuts in each row.
3. 5 rows of 7 coconuts make 5 × 7 = 35 coconuts.
4. Now think about sharing the same 35 coconuts. Split them into 7 equal groups: how many are in each group? Split them into 5 equal groups: how many now?
5. Think about it, then try it with the coconut tray on the next screen.

tool_config.title: Coconut Array
tool_config.idea: Build an array of coconuts with a chosen number of rows and columns and read the multiplication fact and the two division facts that go with it: the same coconuts split into equal groups by the columns, or by the rows. This is the free first try of the chapter, so it asks and shows; the videos that follow name the facts.
tool_config.screen: The packing shed table on Susie and Sunitha's coconut farm in Kerala, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A wooden coconut tray fills the middle of the screen and is the largest thing on it: it shows coconuts in rows and columns, up to 9 rows and 9 columns. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Above the tray is a Columns stepper with a plus and a minus button, and beside the tray a Rows stepper. Below the tray is a fact board with three lines: rows × columns = total, total ÷ columns = rows, and total ÷ rows = columns, with empty slots for number cards, and two buttons, Groups by columns and Groups by rows, that outline the groups on the tray in two colours. A sentence under the tray reads, for example, 35 split into 7 groups has 5 in each group. Controls: tap plus or minus on a stepper to add or remove a row or a column; tap a Groups button to outline the groups; drag number cards onto the slots of the fact board; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the fact board of this card), Reset (an empty tray), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the number of rows, the number of columns, the number of coconuts in all, the number of groups and the number in each group, and a card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at the array of 5 rows of 7 coconuts from the story on the coconut tray. Count the rows, count the coconuts in each row, and say how many coconuts there are in all. Then press Next.

Build arrays with the steppers, read the multiplication fact, outline the groups by columns and by rows to read the two division facts, fill a fact board for an array that is given, and build a row of one.
Write the two division facts for the array of the story, using its multiplication fact, and then write the multiplication fact and two division facts for the array of 4 rows of 8 that the tray shows.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): build 4 rows of 6 coconuts with the steppers. How many coconuts are there? Write the multiplication fact. Answer: 24 coconuts, 4 × 6 = 24.

Card 2: press Groups by columns and then Groups by rows. Write the two division facts. Answer: by columns there are 6 groups with 4 in each group, so 24 ÷ 6 = 4; by rows there are 4 groups with 6 in each group, so 24 ÷ 4 = 6.

Card 3 (practice values): build 3 rows of 8 coconuts. Is the total the same as before? Write the three facts. Answer: 3 × 8 = 24, the same 24 coconuts in a different array, and the division facts are 24 ÷ 8 = 3 and 24 ÷ 3 = 8.
Card 4 (practice values): the tray shows 6 rows of 5 coconuts. Fill the fact board with one multiplication fact and two division facts. Answer: 6 × 5 = 30, 30 ÷ 5 = 6 and 30 ÷ 6 = 5.
Card 5 (practice values): build 1 row of 9 coconuts. Write the facts and say what 9 ÷ 1 is. Answer: 1 × 9 = 9, 9 ÷ 9 = 1 and 9 ÷ 1 = 9. Dividing by 1 gives the same number.

Challenge: 'Observe the following array of coconuts. Write two division facts using the given multiplication fact.' The tray shows 5 rows of 7 coconuts and the fact 5 × 7 = 35. Answer: 35 ÷ 7 = 5, because 35 split into 7 groups has 5 in each group; and 35 ÷ 5 = 7, because 35 split into 5 groups has 7 in each group.

Challenge: 'Write the appropriate multiplication fact for the array shown below. Write two division facts that follow from the multiplication fact.' The tray shows 4 rows of 8 coconuts. Answer: 4 × 8 = 32, 32 ÷ 8 = 4 and 32 ÷ 4 = 8. Next stop: the videos name the two division facts.
feedback: A tap on plus adds a row or a column and the coconut count in all changes at once, for example 4 rows of 6 is 24 coconuts in all.
When Groups by columns is pressed the tool outlines the columns and says, for example: 24 split into 6 groups has 4 in each group, so 24 ÷ 6 = 4.
When Groups by rows is pressed the tool outlines the rows and says, for example: 24 split into 4 groups has 6 in each group, so 24 ÷ 4 = 6.
A number card dropped in the wrong slot slides back with a clue, such as: Which number is the total of all the coconuts? A card in the right slot locks in with a soft chime.
A fact that mixes up the numbers gets a soft amber note, for example: The total 24 is the number being split, so it comes first in a division fact.
tool_config.done_when: The student has built the arrays of the cards, written the multiplication fact and both division facts for each, and has written the facts for the two arrays of the story and of 4 rows of 8.

hint_ladder.text: Count the rows and count the coconuts in each row. How many coconuts are there in all?
Split the coconuts into equal groups: one group for each column, or one group for each row. Press a Groups button and see.
The total is the number being split. Write the total, then the sign ÷, then the number of groups, then the number in each group.
For 5 rows of 7: 35 split into 7 groups has 5 in each group, so 35 ÷ 7 = 5. The other fact uses the 5 rows: 35 ÷ 5 = 7.

concepts.concept_name: Two Division Facts from One Multiplication Fact

content.text:
1. Predict first: 3 rows of 9 coconuts make 27. If you split the 27 coconuts into 9 equal groups, how many are in each group? If you split them into 3 equal groups, how many?
2. The array has 3 rows and 9 columns, so the multiplication fact is 3 × 9 = 27.
3. Split the 27 coconuts into 9 equal groups, one group for each column. Each group has 3 coconuts. That is 27 ÷ 9 = 3.
4. Split the same 27 coconuts into 3 equal groups, one group for each row. Each group has 9 coconuts. That is 27 ÷ 3 = 9.
5. Rule: one multiplication fact gives two division facts. Divide the total by one of the two numbers and the answer is the other number.

Worked example: Susie lays out an array of 27 coconuts in 3 rows of 9 (practice values). Write the multiplication fact and the two division facts.
1. Count the rows and the columns: 3 rows and 9 columns.
2. Multiplication fact: 3 × 9 = 27.
3. Split the 27 coconuts into 9 equal groups, one for each column: 3 in each group, so 27 ÷ 9 = 3.
4. Split the 27 coconuts into 3 equal groups, one for each row: 9 in each group, so 27 ÷ 3 = 9.
5. Check: 9 × 3 = 27 and 3 × 9 = 27, so both division facts match the multiplication fact.
Answer: 3 × 9 = 27, 27 ÷ 9 = 3 and 27 ÷ 3 = 9

lines: Dividend (N) = Divisor (D) × Quotient (Q)

content.text:
1. Predict first: in 45 ÷ 5 = 9, which number is being split, which number do we divide by, and which is the answer? Name each one.
2. The number that is split is the dividend (N). The number we divide by is the divisor (D). The answer is the quotient (Q).
3. In 45 ÷ 5 = 9 the dividend is 45, the divisor is 5, and the quotient is 9.
4. Notice: Dividend = Divisor × Quotient. Here 45 = 5 × 9. This is how to check any division.
5. Dividing by 1: 45 ÷ 1 = 45, because 1 × 45 = 45. Dividing by 1 does not make the number smaller.
6. Rule: N = D × Q.

content.text:
Worked example: Name the dividend, divisor and quotient in 45 ÷ 5 = 9, check the fact, and find 45 ÷ 1 (practice values).
1. The dividend (N) is 45, the number that is split.
2. The divisor (D) is 5, the number we divide by.
3. The quotient (Q) is 9, the answer.
4. Check with N = D × Q: 5 × 9 = 45, which is the dividend.
5. Dividing by 1: 45 ÷ 1 asks how many are in each group when 45 is split into 1 group. All 45 are in that one group, so 45 ÷ 1 = 45.
6. Check: 1 × 45 = 45.
Answer: The dividend is 45, the divisor is 5 and the quotient is 9, and 45 ÷ 1 = 45

media.description: Concept video: Show that one multiplication fact gives two division facts: split the total into groups by the columns or by the rows. It works this example: Susie lays out an array of 27 coconuts in 3 rows of 9 (practice values). Write the multiplication fact and the two division facts.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: 3 rows of 9 coconuts make 27. If you split the 27 coconuts into 9 equal groups, how many are in each group? If you split them into 3 equal groups, how many? The array has 3 rows and 9 columns, so the multiplication fact is 3 × 9 = 27. Split the 27 coconuts into 9 equal groups, one group for each column. Each group has 3 coconuts. That is 27 ÷ 9 = 3. Split the same 27 coconuts into 3 equal groups, one group for each row. Each group has 9 coconuts. That is 27 ÷ 3 = 9. Rule: one multiplication fact gives two division facts. Divide the total by one of the two numbers and the answer is the other number. 1. Count the rows and the columns: 3 rows and 9 columns. 2. Multiplication fact: 3 × 9 = 27. 3. Split the 27 coconuts into 9 equal groups, one for each column: 3 in each group, so 27 ÷ 9 = 3. 4. Split the 27 coconuts into 3 equal groups, one for each row: 9 in each group, so 27 ÷ 3 = 9. 5. Check: 9 × 3 = 27 and 3 × 9 = 27, so both division facts match the multiplication fact. Answer: 3 × 9 = 27, 27 ÷ 9 = 3 and 27 ÷ 3 = 9

media.description: Concept video: Name the dividend, the divisor and the quotient, show that Dividend = Divisor × Quotient, and show that dividing by 1 gives the same number. It works this example: Name the dividend, divisor and quotient in 45 ÷ 5 = 9, check the fact, and find 45 ÷ 1 (practice values).
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: in 45 ÷ 5 = 9, which number is being split, which number do we divide by, and which is the answer? Name each one. The number that is split is the dividend (N). The number we divide by is the divisor (D). The answer is the quotient (Q). In 45 ÷ 5 = 9 the dividend is 45, the divisor is 5, and the quotient is 9. Notice: Dividend = Divisor × Quotient. Here 45 = 5 × 9. This is how to check any division. Dividing by 1: 45 ÷ 1 = 45, because 1 × 45 = 45. Dividing by 1 does not make the number smaller. Rule: N = D × Q. 1. The dividend (N) is 45, the number that is split. 2. The divisor (D) is 5, the number we divide by. 3. The quotient (Q) is 9, the answer. 4. Check with N = D × Q: 5 × 9 = 45, which is the dividend. 5. Dividing by 1: 45 ÷ 1 asks how many are in each group when 45 is split into 1 group. All 45 are in that one group, so 45 ÷ 1 = 45. 6. Check: 1 × 45 = 45. Answer: The dividend is 45, the divisor is 5 and the quotient is 9, and 45 ÷ 1 = 45

steps: (a): 30 × 30 = 900. Both numbers are 30, so the two division statements are the same: 900 ÷ 30 = 30.
Relationship: the dividend is the product, and the divisor and the quotient are the two numbers that were multiplied.
content.text:

4. $(d)$: $200 \times 16 = 3200$, so $3200 \div 200 = 16$ and $3200 \div 16 = 200$.

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many groups of 9 are in 270? Start with the table fact 27 ÷ 9 = 3.
2. 270 is 27 tens. The table fact says 27 ÷ 9 = 3, so 27 tens split into groups of 9 gives 3 tens.
3. 3 tens is 30, so 270 ÷ 9 = 30.
4. Check the quotient by multiplying: 9 × 30 = 270.
5. The same works with hundreds. 2700 is 27 hundreds, so 2700 ÷ 9 = 300.
6. Rule: use the table fact, then put back the tens or the hundreds.

3. Check: 9 × 30 = 270.
4. 2700 is 27 hundreds. 27 hundreds split into groups of 9 gives 3 hundreds. So 2700 ÷ 9 = 300.
5. Check: 9 × 300 = 2700.
6. 2700 ÷ 90: 90 is 9 tens, so the answer is the same as for 270 ÷ 9. 2700 ÷ 90 = 30.
7. Check: 90 × 30 = 2700.
Answer: 270 ÷ 9 = 30, 2700 ÷ 9 = 300 and 2700 ÷ 90 = 30

content.text:
1. Predict first: 50 ÷ 10 = 5. What is 500 ÷ 10, and what is 5000 ÷ 10?
2. Look at 70 ÷ 10 = 7, 700 ÷ 10 = 70 and 7000 ÷ 10 = 700. Each time the dividend gets one more zero, the quotient gets one more zero.
3. On a place value chart the digit 7 slides one place to the right each time we divide by 10: from the tens to the ones, from the hundreds to the tens, from the thousands to the hundreds.
4. Dividing by 100 slides the digits two places: 7000 ÷ 100 = 70.
5. When the dividend is the divisor with zeros added, the quotient is 10 or 100: 3500 ÷ 35 = 100, because 35 × 100 = 3500.
6. Rule: dividing by 10 moves every digit one place to the right, and dividing by 100 moves it two places.

content.text:
Worked example: Divide 70, 700 and 7000 by 10, and then divide 3500 by 35 (practice values).
1. 70 ÷ 10 = 7: the 7 tens become 7 ones.
2. 700 ÷ 10 = 70: the 7 hundreds become 7 tens.
3. 7000 ÷ 10 = 700: the 7 thousands become 7 hundreds.
4. Pattern: one more zero in the dividend gives one more zero in the quotient, and the digit 7 moves one place to the right each time.
5. 3500 is 35 with two zeros added, so 3500 ÷ 35 = 100.
6. Check: 35 × 100 = 3500.
Answer: 70 ÷ 10 = 7, 700 ÷ 10 = 70, 7000 ÷ 10 = 700 and 3500 ÷ 35 = 100

2. 700 ÷ 10 = 70: the 7 hundreds become 7 tens.
3. 7000 ÷ 10 = 700: the 7 thousands become 7 hundreds.
4. Pattern: one more zero in the dividend gives one more zero in the quotient, and the digit 7 moves one place to the right each time.
5. 3500 is 35 with two zeros added, so 3500 ÷ 35 = 100.
6. Check: 35 × 100 = 3500.
Answer: 70 ÷ 10 = 7, 700 ÷ 10 = 70, 7000 ÷ 10 = 700 and 3500 ÷ 35 = 100

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: how many groups of 9 are in 270? Start with the table fact 27 ÷ 9 = 3. 270 is 27 tens. The table fact says 27 ÷ 9 = 3, so 27 tens split into groups of 9 gives 3 tens. 3 tens is 30, so 270 ÷ 9 = 30. Check the quotient by multiplying: 9 × 30 = 270. The same works with hundreds. 2700 is 27 hundreds, so 2700 ÷ 9 = 300. Rule: use the table fact, then put back the tens or the hundreds. 1. 270 is 27 tens, and the table fact is 27 ÷ 9 = 3. 2. 27 tens split into groups of 9 gives 3 tens, which is 30. So 270 ÷ 9 = 30. 3. Check: 9 × 30 = 270. 4. 2700 is 27 hundreds. 27 hundreds split into groups of 9 gives 3 hundreds. So 2700 ÷ 9 = 300. 5. Check: 9 × 300 = 2700. 6. 2700 ÷ 90: 90 is 9 tens, so the answer is the same as for 270 ÷ 9. 2700 ÷ 90 = 30. 7. Check: 90 × 30 = 2700. Answer: 270 ÷ 9 = 30, 2700 ÷ 9 = 300 and 2700 ÷ 90 = 30

5. $(e)$: $300 \div 100 = 3$, because $100 \times 3 = 300$.
6. $(f)$: $500 \div 50 = 10$, because $50 \times 10 = 500$.
7. $(g)$: $200 \div 20 = 10$, because $20 \times 10 = 200$.
8. $(h)$: $440 \div 44 = 10$, because $44 \times 10 = 440$.

steps: Name the boxes: top row A ÷ B = C; A − D = F down the left; C × E = H down the right; F + G = H along the bottom.
Start with the division A ÷ B = C. The numbers are from 1 to 8 and each is used once, so try 6 ÷ 3 = 2 and 8 ÷ 4 = 2.
Try 6 ÷ 3 = 2: then A = 6, B = 3, C = 2. Left column: 6 − D = F. Right column: 2 × E = H.
The numbers left are 1, 4, 5, 7 and 8. Try E = 4: 2 × 4 = 8, so H = 8. Then D = 5 gives 6 − 5 = 1, so F = 1, and G = 7 gives 1 + 7 = 8.
First answer: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, 6 − 5 = 1, 2 × 4 = 8, 1 + 7 = 8. All eight numbers 6, 3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 7, 8 are different.
Try 8 ÷ 4 = 2: then A = 8, B = 4, C = 2. Try E = 3: 2 × 3 = 6, so H = 6. Then D = 7 gives 8 − 7 = 1, so F = 1, and G = 5 gives 1 + 5 = 6.
Second answer: 8 ÷ 4 = 2, 8 − 7 = 1, 2 × 3 = 6, 1 + 5 = 6. All eight numbers 8, 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 5, 6 are different.
Trying every placement of 1 to 8 shows there are exactly two answers.

media.title: Let Us Do (division with tens and hundreds), Q4
media.context: Coconut Farm. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Question video: Place the numbers 1 to 8 in the following boxes so that all the four operations, division, multiplication, addition and subtraction are correct. No number must be repeated. How did you think about solving this? Is there more than one answer?
media.teaching_notes: 1. Name the boxes: top row A ÷ B = C; A − D = F down the left; C × E = H down the right; F + G = H along the bottom. 2. Start with the division A ÷ B = C. The numbers are from 1 to 8 and each is used once, so try 6 ÷ 3 = 2 and 8 ÷ 4 = 2. 3. Try 6 ÷ 3 = 2: then A = 6, B = 3, C = 2. Left column: 6 − D = F. Right column: 2 × E = H. 4. The numbers left are 1, 4, 5, 7 and 8. Try E = 4: 2 × 4 = 8, so H = 8. Then D = 5 gives 6 − 5 = 1, so F = 1, and G = 7 gives 1 + 7 = 8. 5. First answer: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, 6 − 5 = 1, 2 × 4 = 8, 1 + 7 = 8. All eight numbers 6, 3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 7, 8 are different. 6. Try 8 ÷ 4 = 2: then A = 8, B = 4, C = 2. Try E = 3: 2 × 3 = 6, so H = 6. Then D = 7 gives 8 − 7 = 1, so F = 1, and G = 5 gives 1 + 5 = 6. 7. Second answer: 8 ÷ 4 = 2, 8 − 7 = 1, 2 × 3 = 6, 1 + 5 = 6. All eight numbers 8, 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 5, 6 are different. 8. Trying every placement of 1 to 8 shows there are exactly two answers. Answer: Yes, two answers: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, 6 − 5 = 1, 2 × 4 = 8, 1 + 7 = 8; or 8 ÷ 4 = 2, 8 − 7 = 1, 2 × 3 = 6, 1 + 5 = 6

The book's hints: 10 × ___ = 1000 and 37 × ___ = 3700.
steps: Pattern: take the zeros of the divisor away from the zeros of the dividend and use the table fact.
content.text:
1. $(a)$: $1000 \div 10 = 100$, because $10 \times 100 = 1000$.
2. $(b)$: $1000 \div 100 = 10$, because $100 \times 10 = 1000$.
3. $(c)$: $1600$ is $16$ hundreds, and $16 \div 4 = 4$, so $1600 \div 4 = 400$.
4. $(d)$: $2000$ is $2$ thousands, and $2 \div 2 = 1$, so $2000 \div 2 = 1000$.
5. $(e)$: $2000 \div 20 = 100$, because $20 \times 100 = 2000$.
6. $(f)$: $3700 \div 37 = 100$, because $37 \times 100 = 3700$.
7. $(g)$: $3300$ is $33$ hundreds, and $33 \div 3 = 11$, so $3300 \div 3 = 1100$.
8. $(h)$: $3300 \div 300 = 11$, because $300 \times 11 = 3300$.
[Image: Patterns in Division and Place Value: Ans1: solution]
9. (i): $4000 \div 40 = 100$, because $40 \times 100 = 4000$.
10. Pattern: take the zeros of the divisor away from the zeros of the dividend and use the table fact.

concepts.concept_name: Split the Number into Convenient Parts

content.text: I can split the number into convenient parts.
content.publication_text: I can split the number into convenient parts.
lines: I can split the number into convenient parts.

content.text:
1. Predict first: 2856 ÷ 7 looks hard. Can you cut 2856 into two parts that 7 divides easily?
2. Split 2856 into 2800 + 56. Both parts are easy to divide by 7.
3. 2800 ÷ 7 = 400, because 28 ÷ 7 = 4 and there are two zeros. And 56 ÷ 7 = 8.
4. Put the answers together: 400 + 8 = 408. So 2856 ÷ 7 = 408.
5. Check the answer: 7 × 408 = 2856.
6. Rule: split the number into parts the divisor divides easily, divide each part, then add the answers.

3. 2800 ÷ 7 = 400 and 56 ÷ 7 = 8.
4. Put the answers together: 400 + 8 = 408.
5. Check: 7 × 408 = 2856.

content.text: I can do it in a different way.
content.publication_text: I can do it in a different way.
lines: I can do it in a different way.

content.text:
1. Predict first: 2994 is just 6 less than 3000. How could 3000 help you find 2994 ÷ 3?
2. Write 2994 = 3000 − 6. The number 3000 is easy to divide by 3.
3. 3000 ÷ 3 = 1000, and the extra part is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.
4. The 6 was added to reach 3000, so take its share away: 1000 − 2 = 998.
5. Check the answer: 3 × 998 = 2994.
6. Rule: round up to an easy number, divide, then take away the share of the extra.

content.text: To divide by 4, I can halve twice.
content.publication_text: To divide by 4, I can halve twice.
lines: To divide by 4, I can halve twice.

content.text:
1. Predict first: how can you divide 264 by 4 using only halves?
2. Dividing by 4 is the same as halving twice, because 2 × 2 = 4.
3. Half of 264 is 132. Half of 132 is 66. So 264 ÷ 4 = 66.
4. Check the answer: 4 × 66 = 264.
5. Dividing by 8 is halving three times, because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. For example 216 ÷ 8: halves 108, 54 and 27.
6. Rule: halve once to divide by 2, twice to divide by 4 and three times to divide by 8.

media.title: Smart Splitter

tool_config.title: Smart Splitter
tool_config.idea: Divide in the head by cutting the dividend into convenient parts, a sum or a difference, dividing each part and putting the answers together, and by halving again and again for the divisors 4 and 8. Choosing where to cut the number is the whole strategy.
tool_config.screen: The tally board in the packing shed on Susie and Sunitha's coconut farm, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A long number bar for the dividend is the largest thing on screen, with its number written on it. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. A cutter with a handle slides along the bar to set the cut, and a Plus and Minus switch decides if the number is cut into two parts that add up to it or is a round bar with a small piece taken off. Under the cut are two small bars for the two parts, each with a divisor dial and an empty box for its quotient, and an answer slot where the two quotients are put together. For halving there is a chain of boxes with a Halve button between them. Controls: drag the cutter; tap Plus or Minus; type each part divided by the divisor; tap Halve to fill the next box; type the final answer; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the cut of this card), Reset (returns the whole bar), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the dividend, the divisor, the two parts and a line that shows whether the parts give the dividend again, and a card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at the bar for 2856 from the video, cut into 2800 and 56 (practice values). Say why 7 divides both parts easily. Then press Next.
Cut a number where the divisor divides both parts easily, with a plus split or a minus split, divide each part and put the answers together; then halve a number two and three times.
Fill the book's boxes for the divisions of Try It!, first the four with the split boxes and then the two with the halving boxes.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): 3,654 ÷ 6 with a plus split. Answer: 3,654 = 3,600 + 54, 3,600 ÷ 6 = 600 and 54 ÷ 6 = 9, so 600 + 9 = 609. Check: 6 × 609 = 3,654.
Card 2 (practice values): 1,484 ÷ 7 with a plus split. Answer: 1,484 = 1,400 + 84, 1,400 ÷ 7 = 200 and 84 ÷ 7 = 12, so 200 + 12 = 212. Check: 7 × 212 = 1,484.
Card 3 (practice values): 4,995 ÷ 5 with a minus split. Answer: 4,995 = 5,000 − 5, 5,000 ÷ 5 = 1,000 and 5 ÷ 5 = 1, so 1,000 − 1 = 999. Check: 5 × 999 = 4,995.
Card 4 (practice values): 392 ÷ 4 by halving twice. Answer: half of 392 is 196 and half of 196 is 98, so 392 ÷ 4 = 98. Check: 4 × 98 = 392.
Card 5 (practice values): 520 ÷ 8 by halving three times. Answer: 260, 130 and 65, so 520 ÷ 8 = 65. Check: 8 × 65 = 520.

Challenge: 'Try It!' with the split boxes: 64 ÷ 4, 265 ÷ 5, 1560 ÷ 8 and 4824 ÷ 24 (a plus sign in the first, second and fourth, a minus sign in the third). Answer: for example 64 = 40 + 24 gives 10 + 6 = 16; 265 = 250 + 15 gives 50 + 3 = 53; 1560 = 1600 − 40 gives 200 − 5 = 195; 4824 = 4800 + 24 gives 200 + 1 = 201. Other splits may also be right.

Challenge: 'Try It!' with the halving boxes: 168 ÷ 8 with the boxes Halve 168, Halve ___ and Halve ___, and 144 ÷ 4 with the boxes Halve 144 and Halve ___. Answer: 168, 84, 42, 21, so 168 ÷ 8 = 21; and 144, 72, 36, so 144 ÷ 4 = 36. Next stop: Susie's farm.
feedback: A cut at a place where the divisor does not divide a part gets a soft amber note, for example: 7 does not divide 2855 easily. Slide the cutter to 2800.
When both parts are divided the tool joins the answers and says, for example: 400 and 8 together make 408, and 7 × 408 = 2856.
In minus mode the tool shows the round bar with a small piece taken off, and says: 5,000 is 5 more than 4,995, so take the share of 5 away at the end.
Each press of Halve fills the next box and shows the half, for example half of 392 is 196.
A part divided wrongly slides back with a clue such as: Check by multiplying. What times 6 is 3,600?
tool_config.done_when: The student has cut and divided the numbers of the cards by splitting and by halving, and has filled the book's boxes for Try It!.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students split a dividend into convenient parts that the divisor divides easily, divide each part, and add the answers to find the quotient.
Students divide by rounding the dividend up to an easy number, dividing it, and taking the share of the extra part away from the answer.
Students divide a number by 4 or by 8 by halving it two or three times, and check the answer by multiplying.
Students use smart mental methods, split, round up or halve, to solve the book's divisions, give examples of their own, and check each answer by multiplying.

steps: Choose a divisor, then split the number into a round part and a small part that the divisor divides easily.

content.text:
1. Choose a divisor, then split the number into a round part and a small part that the divisor divides easily.
2. $906 \div 3$: $906 = 900 + 6$, $900 \div 3 = 300$ and $6 \div 3 = 2$, so $300 + 2 = 302$.
3. $2412 \div 6$: $2412 = 2400 + 12$, $2400 \div 6 = 400$ and $12 \div 6 = 2$, so $400 + 2 = 402$.
4. $3515 \div 5$: $3515 = 3500 + 15$, $3500 \div 5 = 700$ and $15 \div 5 = 3$, so $700 + 3 = 703$.
5. $4812 \div 4$: $4812 = 4800 + 12$, $4800 \div 4 = 1200$ and $12 \div 4 = 3$, so $1200 + 3 = 1203$.
6. $6309 \div 3$: $6309 = 6300 + 9$, $6300 \div 3 = 2100$ and $9 \div 3 = 3$, so $2100 + 3 = 2103$.
7. Many other examples work. Check each answer by multiplying.
Answer: Sample answer: $906 \div 3 = 302$, $2412 \div 6 = 402$, $3515 \div 5 = 703$, $4812 \div 4 = 1203$, $6309 \div 3 = 2103$. Your answer may differ

content.book_number: Mental Strategies: when repeated halving works
content.question: For which other divisors and dividend might this strategy of repeated halving work?
steps: Halving twice divides by 4. Halving three times divides by 8. Halving four times divides by 16, because 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.
So repeated halving works for the divisors 2, 4, 8 and 16.
The dividend must be able to be halved that many times with whole-number halves.
Example: 96 ÷ 8 by halving three times: 48, 24, 12, so 96 ÷ 8 = 12. Check: 8 × 12 = 96.
Example: 240 ÷ 16 by halving four times: 120, 60, 30, 15, so 240 ÷ 16 = 15. Check: 16 × 15 = 240.
It does not work for a divisor like 5 or 6, because halving does not divide by 5 or by 6.

concepts.concept_name: Take Away Groups of the Divisor

content.text: Susie and Sunitha have a large coconut farm and they have harvested 1,117 coconuts in April.
content.publication_text: Susie and Sunitha have a large coconut farm and they have harvested 1,117 coconuts in April.
lines: Susie and Sunitha have a large coconut farm and they have harvested 1,117 coconuts in April.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Susie packs 378 coconuts into groups of 6. If she takes away 20 groups of 6 each time, how many times can she do it?
2. She takes away 20 groups of 6, which is 6 × 20 = 120 coconuts. She does it again and again until the coconuts run out.
3. 378 − 120 = 258, then 258 − 120 = 138, then 138 − 120 = 18. Now 3 groups of 6 take away the last 18.
4. The groups taken away: 20 + 20 + 20 + 3 = 63. So 378 ÷ 6 = 63.
5. Check the answer: 6 × 63 = 378.
6. Rule: take away groups of the divisor, add up how many groups you took, and that is the quotient.

content.text:
Worked example: Susie packs 378 coconuts into groups of 6 (practice values). Find 378 ÷ 6 by taking away groups.
1. Take away 20 groups of 6: 6 × 20 = 120, and 378 − 120 = 258.
2. Take away 20 groups of 6: 6 × 20 = 120, and 258 − 120 = 138.
3. Take away 20 groups of 6: 6 × 20 = 120, and 138 − 120 = 18.
4. Take away 3 groups of 6: 6 × 3 = 18, and 18 − 18 = 0.
5. Add the groups taken away: 20 + 20 + 20 + 3 = 63.
6. Nothing is left, so 378 ÷ 6 = 63.
7. Check: 6 × 63 = 378.
Answer: 378 ÷ 6 = 63

concepts.concept_name: Choose the Biggest Group That Fits

content.text:
Estimate the answer first. Do you realise that each customer will likely get less than 100 coconuts?
Do you think Sunitha's method is better? Discuss which one you would prefer and why.
content.publication_text:

lines: Estimate the answer first. Do you realise that each customer will likely get less than 100 coconuts?
Do you think Sunitha's method is better? Discuss which one you would prefer and why.

content.text:
1. Predict first: for 861 ÷ 7, is the answer more or less than 100? Is it more or less than 200?
2. Estimate first: 7 × 100 = 700 is less than 861 and 7 × 200 = 1400 is more, so the answer is between 100 and 200.
3. Take away the biggest group that fits. 100 groups of 7 is 700, and 861 − 700 = 161. Then 20 groups of 7 is 140, and 161 − 140 = 21. Then 3 groups of 7 is 21, and 21 − 21 = 0.
4. 100 + 20 + 3 = 123, in only 3 steps. So 861 ÷ 7 = 123.
5. A group that is too big cannot be taken away: 200 groups of 7 is 1400, which is more than 861.
6. Rule: estimate first, then take away the biggest tens or hundreds of groups that fit.

Worked example: Find 861 ÷ 7 by estimating first and taking away the biggest groups that fit (practice values).
1. Estimate: 7 × 100 = 700 and 7 × 200 = 1400, so the answer is between 100 and 200.
2. 200 groups are too big, because 1400 is more than 861.
3. Take away 100 groups of 7: 7 × 100 = 700, and 861 − 700 = 161.
4. Take away 20 groups of 7: 7 × 20 = 140, and 161 − 140 = 21.
5. Take away 3 groups of 7: 7 × 3 = 21, and 21 − 21 = 0.
6. Add the groups taken away: 100 + 20 + 3 = 123.
7. Nothing is left, so 861 ÷ 7 = 123.
8. Check: 7 × 123 = 861.
Answer: 861 ÷ 7 = 123

content.text:
1. Predict first: for 487 ÷ 9, after you take away all the groups of 9 that fit, will anything be left over?
2. Take away 50 groups of 9, which is 450: 487 − 450 = 37. Take away 4 groups of 9, which is 36: 37 − 36 = 1.
3. The 1 that is left is smaller than 9, so no more groups of 9 can be taken away. It is the remainder (R).
4. The quotient is 50 + 4 = 54, so 487 ÷ 9: quotient 54, remainder 1.
5. Check with N = D × Q + R: 9 × 54 + 1 = 487.
6. Rule: N = D × Q + R, and the remainder is always less than the divisor.

tool_config.title: Take Away Groups
tool_config.idea: Divide by taking away groups of the divisor from a pile again and again, record the groups taken away as partial quotients, see that a group that is too big cannot be taken away, read what is left as the remainder, and check the division with N = D × Q + R.
tool_config.screen: A pile of coconuts at the packing shed on Susie and Sunitha's farm, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The pile and its number are the largest things on screen, with a row of empty bags beside it. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Three take-away buttons sit under the pile: Take 100 groups, Take 10 groups and Take 1 group, each of the divisor; pressing one removes that many groups of coconuts from the pile and the number left changes at once. The book's layout fills in on the right, one subtraction under another, with the group counts added up along the top, for example 100 + 80 + 1. A remainder counter shows what is left, and an N = D × Q + R board below has slots for D, Q and R. An estimate bar above the pile asks if the answer is less than 100 or between 100 and 200. Controls: tap a take-away button; tap Undo; set the estimate; type D, Q and R into the board; Check, Hint, Retry (restores the pile of this card), Reset (a new pile), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the dividend, the divisor, the coconuts left, the groups taken so far, and a card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at the pile of 378 coconuts and the bags of 6 from the video (practice values). Say how many groups of 6 you could take away first. Then press Next.

Take away groups from a pile, try a group that is too big and see why it cannot be taken, estimate first and take the biggest groups that fit, divide by a two-digit number, and write the remainder rule.
Fill the blanks of the book's two divisions, 726 ÷ 4 and 902 ÷ 16, and answer the book's questions about N = D × Q + R.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): 456 ÷ 6 in two takes. Answer: take 70 groups, 6 × 70 = 420 and 456 − 420 = 36; take 6 groups, 6 × 6 = 36 and 36 − 36 = 0. 70 + 6 = 76. Check: 6 × 76 = 456.

Card 2 (practice values): 509 ÷ 7. Try Take 100 groups first. Answer: 7 × 100 = 700 is more than 509, so it is too big. Take 70 groups: 7 × 70 = 490 and 509 − 490 = 19. Take 2 groups: 7 × 2 = 14 and 19 − 14 = 5. Quotient 72, remainder 5.

Card 3 (practice values): estimate 845 ÷ 5 first, then divide. Answer: 5 × 100 = 500 is less than 845 and 5 × 200 = 1000 is more, so the answer is between 100 and 200. Take 100 groups: 845 − 500 = 345. Take 60 groups: 345 − 300 = 45. Take 9 groups: 45 − 45 = 0. 100 + 60 + 9 = 169. Check: 5 × 169 = 845.
Card 4 (practice values): 372 ÷ 12 with a two-digit divisor. Answer: take 30 groups, 12 × 30 = 360 and 372 − 360 = 12; take 1 group, 12 − 12 = 0. 30 + 1 = 31. Check: 12 × 31 = 372.
Card 5 (practice values): write the remainder rule for 509 ÷ 7. Answer: D = 7, Q = 72, R = 5, so 509 = 7 × 72 + 5, and the remainder 5 is less than the divisor 7.

Challenge: 'Let Us Learn to Divide' 726 ÷ 4: the quotient parts are 100 + ___ + ___, take away ___ first and 326 is left, take away 320 and 6 is left, take away ___ and 2 is left. 'Could we have written 200 here?' Answer: the blanks are 400, 80, 4 and 1, so 100 + 80 + 1 = 181 with remainder 2; 200 is too big because 4 × 200 = 800 is more than 726.

Challenge: 902 ÷ 16: the quotient parts are ___ + 6, take away 800, then 96, and 6 is left. 'What should we write here so that we get a number close to 902 but less than it? Could we have multiplied 16 by a larger tens?' Then the book's questions, with the equal sign of the book written in words: 'Is 726 the same as 4 × 181? Yes/No. So, 726 is 4 × 181 plus ___. Is 902 the same as 16 × 56? Yes/No. So, 902 is 16 × 56 plus ___.' Answer: the blank is 50, so quotient 56 and remainder 6; 16 × 60 = 960 is more than 902. No and No: 726 = 4 × 181 + 2 and 902 = 16 × 56 + 6, so N = D × Q + R. Next stop: the coconut oil.
feedback: A group that is too big stays in the pile and the tool says, for example: 700 is more than the 509 coconuts left. Take away a smaller group.
After each take-away the layout shows the subtraction and the number left, for example 509 − 490 = 19.
When nothing is left the tool adds the groups, for example 70 + 6 = 76, and shows 6 × 76 = 456.
When some coconuts are left that are fewer than the divisor, the tool says: 5 is less than 7, so no more groups of 7 can be taken. 5 is the remainder.
A wrong D, Q or R on the board slides back with a clue such as: The remainder must be less than the divisor.

content.question: Susie and Sunitha have a large coconut farm and they have harvested 1,117 coconuts in April. They sold 582 coconuts equally to 6 regular customers. How many coconuts did each customer get? They sold 582 ÷ 6 coconuts to each customer.
steps: Susie's way: take away groups of 6 again and again.
Take away 20 groups of 6: 6 × 20 = 120, and 582 − 120 = 462.
Take away 20 groups of 6: 6 × 20 = 120, and 462 − 120 = 342.
Take away 20 groups of 6: 6 × 20 = 120, and 342 − 120 = 222.
Take away 20 groups of 6: 6 × 20 = 120, and 222 − 120 = 102.
Take away 10 groups of 6: 6 × 10 = 60, and 102 − 60 = 42.
Take away 7 groups of 6: 6 × 7 = 42, and 42 − 42 = 0.
Add the groups taken away: 20 + 20 + 20 + 20 + 10 + 7 = 97.
Nothing is left, so 582 ÷ 6 = 97.
Sunitha's way: take away the biggest groups that fit. 6 × 90 = 540 is less than 582, so take away 90 groups: 582 − 540 = 42.
Then take away 7 groups of 6: 6 × 7 = 42, and 42 − 42 = 0.
90 + 7 = 97. Both ways give 97 coconuts. Sunitha's way takes 2 steps and Susie's way takes 6 steps.
Estimate check: 6 × 100 = 600 is more than 582, so each customer gets less than 100 coconuts.

content.question: Sometimes, the divisor (D) does not completely divide the dividend (N) and leaves a remainder (R). What is the relationship between the dividend (N) and divisor (D), quotient (Q), and remainder (R)? Try to find out! Is 726 = 4 × 181? Yes/No. So, 726 = 4 × 181 + ___. Is 902 = 16 × 56? content.text:
In a particular year, Susie and Sunitha used 4376 coconuts for extracting coconut oil. They can extract 1 litre of oil from 8 coconuts.
Let us take away maximum groups of 23 in multiples of hundreds and tens.
What would happen if 23 is multiplied by 300 or 500?

content.text:
1. Predict first: for 6534 ÷ 18, which groups can you take away first: hundreds of groups, tens of groups or ones?
2. Start with the biggest. 18 × 300 = 5400 is less than 6534, and 18 × 400 = 7200 is more, so take away 300 groups: 6534 − 5400 = 1134.
3. Next, 18 × 60 = 1080 fits in 1134: 1134 − 1080 = 54.
4. Last, 18 × 3 = 54: 54 − 54 = 0.
5. 300 + 60 + 3 = 363, so 6534 ÷ 18 = 363. Check: 363 × 18 = 6534.
6. Rule: take away hundreds of groups, then tens, then ones, always the biggest that fits.

content.text:
Worked example: Find 6534 ÷ 18 by taking away hundreds, tens and ones groups (practice values).
1. Try the hundreds first: 18 × 400 = 7200 is more than 6534, so 400 groups are too big. 18 × 300 = 5400 fits.
2. Take away 300 groups of 18: 18 × 300 = 5400, and 6534 − 5400 = 1134.
3. Take away 60 groups of 18: 18 × 60 = 1080, and 1134 − 1080 = 54.
4. Take away 3 groups of 18: 18 × 3 = 54, and 54 − 54 = 0.
5. Add the groups taken away: 300 + 60 + 3 = 363.
6. Nothing is left, so 6534 ÷ 18 = 363.
7. Check: 18 × 363 = 6534.
Answer: 6534 ÷ 18 = 363

steps: Guess first: 23 × 400 = 9200 is close to 9913, and 23 × 500 = 11500 is more than 9913.
So 500 groups are too big. 23 × 300 = 6900 fits, but 400 groups fit too, so take the biggest.
Take away 30 groups of 23: 23 × 30 = 690, and 713 − 690 = 23.
Take away 1 group of 23: 23 × 1 = 23, and 23 − 23 = 0.
Add the groups taken away: 400 + 30 + 1 = 431.
Nothing is left, so 9913 ÷ 23 = 431.
So the farm sold 431 kg of coconut husk in May.

steps: Money earned = litres × price for 1 litre = 547 × 175.
Split 175 into 100 + 70 + 5.
Add the three parts: 54700 + 38290 + 2735 = 95725.
Check by estimating: 500 × 200 = 100000, and 95725 is close to it.

2. Split $175$ into $100 + 70 + 5$.
3. $547 \times 100 = 54700$.
4. $547 \times 70 = 38290$.
5. $547 \times 5 = 2735$.
6. Add the three parts: $54700 + 38290 + 2735 = 95725$.
7. Check by estimating: $500 \times 200 = 100000$, and $95725$ is close to it.
Answer: ₹$95725$

Check another way: each coconut gave 35 − 20 = 15 rupees extra, and 254 × 15 = 3810.

content.text: Sunitha's mother has 62 candies to be distributed equally among 5 children. How many candies would each child get? She shows the following way of doing division using place value.

lines: Sunitha's mother has 62 candies to be distributed equally among 5 children. How many candies would each child get? She shows the following way of doing division using place value.

content.text:
1. Predict first: 83 candies are shared equally among 6 children. Can the 8 tens be shared among 6 without breaking a ten?
2. 83 is 8 tens and 3 ones. Share the 8 tens among 6 children: each child gets 1 ten, and 2 tens are left.
3. The 2 tens left cannot be shared without breaking them, so regroup them into 20 ones. With the 3 ones that makes 23 ones.
4. Share the 23 ones among 6 children: each child gets 3 ones, because 6 × 3 = 18, and 5 ones are left.
5. Each child gets 1 ten and 3 ones, which is 13, and 5 candies are left. So 83 ÷ 6: quotient 13, remainder 5.
6. Check: 83 = 6 × 13 + 5.
7. Rule: share the tens, regroup the tens left into ones, then share the ones.

Each child gets 1 ten and 3 ones, which is 13, and 5 candies are left. So 83 ÷ 6: quotient 13, remainder 5.
Rule: share the tens, regroup the tens left into ones, then share the ones.

content.text:
1. Predict first: in 412 ÷ 4, can the 1 ten be shared among 4 equal parts? What should the tens digit of the answer be?
2. 412 is 4 hundreds, 1 ten and 2 ones. Share the 4 hundreds among 4 parts: 1 hundred each.
3. The 1 ten cannot be shared among 4 parts without breaking it, so each part gets 0 tens. Write 0 in the tens place.
4. Regroup the 1 ten into 10 ones. With the 2 ones that makes 12 ones. Share them among 4 parts: 3 ones each, because 4 × 3 = 12.
5. So 412 ÷ 4 = 103. The 0 holds the tens place, and 103 is not 13.
6. How many digits? For a one-digit divisor: if the first digit of the dividend is at least the divisor, the quotient has as many digits as the dividend. If it is less, the quotient has one digit fewer.
7. 412 has the first digit 4, and 4 is at least 4, so the quotient has 3 digits. For 215 ÷ 4 the first digit 2 is less than 4, so the quotient has 2 digits.
8. Check: 4 × 103 = 412.

content.text:
Worked example: Find 412 ÷ 4 by place value (practice values), and say how many digits the quotient has.
1. Start with the 4 hundreds. Share 4 hundreds among 4 equal parts: 1 hundred each, because 4 × 1 = 4, and nothing is left.
2. Nothing is left from the hundreds. Bring down the 1 ten: 1 ten to share. 1 ten cannot be shared among 4 equal parts, so each part gets 0 tens: write 0.
3. 1 ten left, regrouped as 10 ones; with the 2 ones that makes 12 ones to share. Share 12 ones among 4 equal parts: 3 ones each, because 4 × 3 = 12, and nothing is left.
4. The quotient digits are 1, 0, 3, so 412 ÷ 4 = 103.
5. Check: 4 × 103 = 412.
6. Digits: the first digit of 412 is 4, which is at least the divisor 4, so the quotient has 3 digits, as many as the dividend.
7. Compare 215 ÷ 4: the first digit 2 is less than 4, so the quotient has one digit fewer. 215 ÷ 4: quotient 53, remainder 3. Check: 215 = 4 × 53 + 3.
Answer: 412 ÷ 4 = 103, with 3 digits

content.text:
1. Predict first: for 3,648 ÷ 12, will taking away groups and place value give the same answer?
2. Taking away groups: 12 × 300 = 3,600, and 3,648 − 3,600 = 48. Then 12 × 4 = 48. So 300 + 4 = 304.
3. Place value: 36 hundreds shared among 12 parts gives 3 hundreds each, because 12 × 3 = 36.
4. The 4 tens cannot be shared among 12 parts, so each part gets 0 tens. The 0 holds the tens place. Then 48 ones shared among 12 parts gives 4 ones each.
5. Both ways give 304. The 0 in 304 is the tens place that had nothing to share.
6. Check: 12 × 304 = 3,648.
7. Rule: both methods give the same quotient. Write 0 in every place that cannot be shared.

content.text:
Worked example: Find 3,648 ÷ 12 in two ways (practice values).
1. First way: take away groups of 12.
2. Take away 300 groups of 12: 12 × 300 = 3,600, and 3,648 − 3,600 = 48.
3. Take away 4 groups of 12: 12 × 4 = 48, and 48 − 48 = 0.
4. Add the groups taken away: 300 + 4 = 304.
5. Nothing is left, so 3,648 ÷ 12 = 304.
6. Check: 12 × 304 = 3,648.
7. Second way: by place value.
8. Start with the 3 thousands. 3 thousands cannot be shared among 12 equal parts, so each part gets 0 thousands: write 0.
9. 3 thousands left, regrouped as 30 hundreds; with the 6 hundreds that makes 36 hundreds to share. Share 36 hundreds among 12 equal parts: 3 hundreds each, because 12 × 3 = 36, and nothing is left.
10. Nothing is left from the hundreds. Bring down the 4 tens: 4 tens to share. 4 tens cannot be shared among 12 equal parts, so each part gets 0 tens: write 0.
11. 4 tens left, regrouped as 40 ones; with the 8 ones that makes 48 ones to share. Share 48 ones among 12 equal parts: 4 ones each, because 12 × 4 = 48, and nothing is left.
12. The quotient digits are 0, 3, 0, 4, so 3,648 ÷ 12 = 304.
13. Check: 12 × 304 = 3,648.
14. Both ways give 304.
Answer: 3,648 ÷ 12 = 304

tool_config.screen: The packing shed table on Susie and Sunitha's coconut farm, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A tray of base ten blocks is the largest thing on screen: flat blocks for hundreds (orange), rods for tens (blue) and small cubes for ones (pink), as the book colours them. Beside the tray stand 2 to 9 empty plates, one for each equal part, and a remainder tray. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. A strip under the plates has the columns thousands, hundreds, tens and ones for the quotient digits, and the long-division record of the book fills in beside it step by step. Controls: press Share for a place to deal that place's blocks to the plates one by one; press Regroup to break one hundred into 10 tens or one ten into 10 ones; drag a block to a plate or to the remainder tray; type a digit into the strip; Check, Hint, Retry (restores the blocks of this card), Reset (clears the table), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Share the 8 tens among 6 children: each child gets 1 ten, and 2 tens are left. The 2 tens left cannot be shared without breaking them, so regroup them into 20 ones. With the 3 ones that makes 23 ones. Share the 23 ones among 6 children: each child gets 3 ones, because 6 × 3 = 18, and 5 ones are left. Each child gets 1 ten and 3 ones, which is 13, and 5 candies are left. So 83 ÷ 6: quotient 13, remainder 5. Check: 83 = 6 × 13 + 5. Rule: share the tens, regroup the tens left into ones, then share the ones. 1. Start with the 8 tens. Share 8 tens among 6 equal parts: 1 ten each, because 6 × 1 = 6, and 2 tens left. 2. 2 tens left, regrouped as 20 ones; with the 3 ones that makes 23 ones to share. Share 23 ones among 6 equal parts: 3 ones each, because 6 × 3 = 18, and 5 ones left. 3. The quotient digits are 1, 3, so the quotient is 13 and the remainder is 5. 4. Check: 83 = 6 × 13 + 5. Answer: Each child gets 13 candies and 5 are left over

media.description: Concept video: Show how to regroup hundreds into tens, why a place that cannot be shared gets a 0, and how many digits the quotient has. It works this example: Find 412 ÷ 4 by place value (practice values), and say how many digits the quotient has.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: in 412 ÷ 4, can the 1 ten be shared among 4 equal parts? What should the tens digit of the answer be? 412 is 4 hundreds, 1 ten and 2 ones. Share the 4 hundreds among 4 parts: 1 hundred each. The 1 ten cannot be shared among 4 parts without breaking it, so each part gets 0 tens. Write 0 in the tens place. Regroup the 1 ten into 10 ones. With the 2 ones that makes 12 ones. Share them among 4 parts: 3 ones each, because 4 × 3 = 12. So 412 ÷ 4 = 103. The 0 holds the tens place, and 103 is not 13. How many digits? For a one-digit divisor: if the first digit of the dividend is at least the divisor, the quotient has as many digits as the dividend. If it is less, the quotient has one digit fewer. 412 has the first digit 4, and 4 is at least 4, so the quotient has 3 digits. For 215 ÷ 4 the first digit 2 is less than 4, so the quotient has 2 digits. Check: 4 × 103 = 412. 1. Start with the 4 hundreds. Share 4 hundreds among 4 equal parts: 1 hundred each, because 4 × 1 = 4, and nothing is left. 2. Nothing is left from the hundreds. Bring down the 1 ten: 1 ten to share. 1 ten cannot be shared among 4 equal parts, so each part gets 0 tens: write 0. 3. 1 ten left, regrouped as 10 ones; with the 2 ones that makes 12 ones to share. Share 12 ones among 4 equal parts: 3 ones each, because 4 × 3 = 12, and nothing is left. 4. The quotient digits are 1, 0, 3, so 412 ÷ 4 = 103. 5. Check: 4 × 103 = 412. 6. Digits: the first digit of 412 is 4, which is at least the divisor 4, so the quotient has 3 digits, as many as the dividend. 7. Compare 215 ÷ 4: the first digit 2 is less than 4, so the quotient has one digit fewer. 215 ÷ 4: quotient 53, remainder 3. Check: 215 = 4 × 53 + 3. Answer: 412 ÷ 4 = 103, with 3 digits

media.description: Concept video: Show that taking away groups and place value give the same quotient for thousands and two-digit divisors, and where the zero goes. It works this example: Find 3,648 ÷ 12 in two ways (practice values).
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: for 3,648 ÷ 12, will taking away groups and place value give the same answer? Taking away groups: 12 × 300 = 3,600, and 3,648 − 3,600 = 48. Then 12 × 4 = 48. So 300 + 4 = 304. Place value: 36 hundreds shared among 12 parts gives 3 hundreds each, because 12 × 3 = 36. The 4 tens cannot be shared among 12 parts, so each part gets 0 tens. The 0 holds the tens place. Then 48 ones shared among 12 parts gives 4 ones each. Both ways give 304. The 0 in 304 is the tens place that had nothing to share. Check: 12 × 304 = 3,648. Rule: both methods give the same quotient. Write 0 in every place that cannot be shared. 1. First way: take away groups of 12. 2. Take away 300 groups of 12: 12 × 300 = 3,600, and 3,648 − 3,600 = 48. 3. Take away 4 groups of 12: 12 × 4 = 48, and 48 − 48 = 0. 4. Add the groups taken away: 300 + 4 = 304. 5. Nothing is left, so 3,648 ÷ 12 = 304. 6. Check: 12 × 304 = 3,648. 7. Second way: by place value. 8. Start with the 3 thousands. 3 thousands cannot be shared among 12 equal parts, so each part gets 0 thousands: write 0. 9. 3 thousands left, regrouped as 30 hundreds; with the 6 hundreds that makes 36 hundreds to share. Share 36 hundreds among 12 equal parts: 3 hundreds each, because 12 × 3 = 36, and nothing is left. 10. Nothing is left from the hundreds. Bring down the 4 tens: 4 tens to share. 4 tens cannot be shared among 12 equal parts, so each part gets 0 tens: write 0. 11. 4 tens left, regrouped as 40 ones; with the 8 ones that makes 48 ones to share. Share 48 ones among 12 equal parts: 4 ones each, because 12 × 4 = 48, and nothing is left. 12. The quotient digits are 0, 3, 0, 4, so 3,648 ÷ 12 = 304. 13. Check: 12 × 304 = 3,648. 14. Both ways give 304. Answer: 3,648 ÷ 12 = 304

steps: Start with the 6 tens. Share 6 tens among 5 equal parts: 1 ten each, because 5 × 1 = 5, and 1 ten left.
1 ten left, regrouped as 10 ones; with the 2 ones that makes 12 ones to share. Share 12 ones among 5 equal parts: 2 ones each, because 5 × 2 = 10, and 2 ones left.
The quotient digits are 1, 2, so the quotient is 12 and the remainder is 2.
So each child gets 12 candies and 2 candies are left.

content.question: Can you tell just by looking at the divisor and dividend, how many digits the quotient would have? Look at the problems above and find this out. Explain your thoughts.
steps: Look at the four problems: 62 ÷ 5, 75 ÷ 8, 324 ÷ 3 and 136 ÷ 6.
62 ÷ 5: the first digit 6 is at least 5, and the quotient 12 has 2 digits, as many as 62.
324 ÷ 3: the first digit 3 is at least 3, and the quotient 108 has 3 digits, as many as 324.
75 ÷ 8: the first digit 7 is less than 8, and the quotient 9 has 1 digit, one fewer than 75.
136 ÷ 6: the first digit 1 is less than 6, and the quotient 22 has 2 digits, one fewer than 136.
Rule for a one-digit divisor: if the first digit of the dividend is at least the divisor, the quotient has as many digits as the dividend. If it is less, the quotient has one digit fewer.
content.answer: With a one-digit divisor: as many digits as the dividend if its first digit is at least the divisor, otherwise one fewer

content.book_number: Let Us Divide: (a) 7,032 ÷ 6
content.question: Let Us Divide. (a): 7,032 ÷ 6. First way, taking away groups of 6: the quotient parts are 1,000 + ___ + 70 + ___; take away ___ and 1,032 is left; take away 600 and 432 is left; take away ___ and 12 is left; take away ___ and nothing is left. Second way, by place value: the quotient digits (thousands, hundreds, tens, ones) are 1, 1, 7, 2.
steps: First way: take away groups of 6.
Take away 70 groups of 6: 6 × 70 = 420, and 432 − 420 = 12.
Take away 2 groups of 6: 6 × 2 = 12, and 12 − 12 = 0.
Add the groups taken away: 1,000 + 100 + 70 + 2 = 1,172.
Nothing is left, so 7,032 ÷ 6 = 1,172.
Second way: by place value, one short line for each place.
Thousands: 7 thousands to share among 6, 1 each, 1 thousand left.
Hundreds: 10 hundreds to share among 6, 1 each, 4 hundreds left.
Tens: 43 tens to share among 6, 7 each, 1 ten left.
Ones: 12 ones to share among 6, 2 each, nothing left.
The quotient digits are 1, 1, 7, 2, so 7,032 ÷ 6 = 1,172.
The blanks of the first way are 100 and 2 in the quotient parts, and 6,000, 420 and 12 to take away.
content.text:
1. First way: take away groups of $6$.
2. Take away $1,000$ groups of $6$: $6 \times 1,000 = 6,000$, and $7,032 - 6,000 = 1,032$.
3. Take away $100$ groups of $6$: $6 \times 100 = 600$, and $1,032 - 600 = 432$.
4. Take away $70$ groups of $6$: $6 \times 70 = 420$, and $432 - 420 = 12$.
5. Take away $2$ groups of $6$: $6 \times 2 = 12$, and $12 - 12 = 0$.
6. Add the groups taken away: $1,000 + 100 + 70 + 2 = 1,172$.
7. Nothing is left, so $7,032 \div 6 = 1,172$.
8. Check: $6 \times 1,172 = 7,032$.
[Image: Let Us Divide: Ans1: solution]
9. Second way: by place value, one short line for each place.
10. Thousands: $7$ thousands to share among $6$, $1$ each, $1$ thousand left.
11. Hundreds: $10$ hundreds to share among $6$, $1$ each, $4$ hundreds left.
12. Tens: $43$ tens to share among $6$, $7$ each, $1$ ten left.
13. Ones: $12$ ones to share among $6$, $2$ each, nothing left.
14. The quotient digits are $1$, $1$, $7$, $2$, so $7,032 \div 6 = 1,172$.
15. Check: $6 \times 1,172 = 7,032$.
16. The blanks of the first way are $100$ and $2$ in the quotient parts, and $6,000$, $420$ and $12$ to take away.
Answer: Quotient $1,172$: the blanks are $100$, $2$, $6,000$, $420$ and $12$

Add the groups taken away: 600 + 1 = 601. 5. Nothing is left, so 3,005 ÷ 5 = 601. 6. Check: 5 × 601 = 3,005. 7. Second way: by place value. 8. Thousands: 3 thousands to share among 5, 0 each, 3 thousands left. 9. Hundreds: 30 hundreds to share among 5, 6 each, nothing left. 10. Tens: 0 tens to share among 5, 0 each, nothing left. 11. Ones: 5 ones to share among 5, 1 each, nothing left. 12. The quotient digits are 0, 6, 0, 1, so 3,005 ÷ 5 = 601. 13. Check: 5 × 601 = 3,005. 14. Why the 0? In the tens place there is 0 tens to share among 5 parts, so each part gets 0 tens. Without the 0 the answer would be 61, and 5 × 61 = 305 is not 3,005. Answer: Quotient 601, with the digits 0, 6, 0, 1

content.book_number: Let Us Do (missing numbers), Q1
content.question: Find the missing numbers such that there is no remainder. Remember, there could be more than one solution. Each box shows a divisor, a dividend and a quotient with some digits missing (written ___): (a): 4 into 480, quotient ___ ___ 0; (b): 3 into 906, quotient ___ 0 ___; (c): 20 into 400, quotient ___ 0; (d): 50 into 100___, quotient ___ 0; (e): ___ into 8___8, quotient 2 1 ___; (f): 3 into ___36, quotient 3 ___ ___; (g): ___ into 88, quotient ___ ___; (h): ___ into 9___0, quotient ___ ___ ___; (i): ___ into 180, quotient ___ ___ ___; (j): ___ into 6,480, quotient ___ ___ ___.
steps: Each missing number must make the division exact. Use Dividend = Divisor × Quotient.
(a): 480 ÷ 4 = 120, so the missing digits are 1 and 2.
(b): 906 ÷ 3 = 302, so the missing digits are 3 and 2.
(c): 400 ÷ 20 = 20, so the missing digit is 2.
(d): the dividend 100___ must be a multiple of 50. Only 1000 works, and 1000 ÷ 50 = 20, so the missing digits are 0 and 2.
(e): only the divisor 4 fits. 848 ÷ 4 = 212 (digits 4 and 2) or 868 ÷ 4 = 217 (digits 6 and 7).
(f): the dividend is 936, and 936 ÷ 3 = 312, so the missing digits are 9, 1 and 2.
(g): 88 can be divided exactly by 1, 2, 4 or 8: the quotient is 88, 44, 22 or 11.
(h): there are many answers, for example 950 ÷ 5 = 190, 920 ÷ 2 = 460, 930 ÷ 3 = 310 and 990 ÷ 9 = 110.
(i): a quotient with 3 digits needs the divisor 1, and 180 ÷ 1 = 180.
Check by multiplying back, for example 4 × 120 = 480 and 8 × 810 = 6,480.
content.text:
1. Each missing number must make the division exact. Use Dividend $=$ Divisor $\times$ Quotient.
2. $(a)$: $480 \div 4 = 120$, so the missing digits are $1$ and $2$.
3. $(b)$: $906 \div 3 = 302$, so the missing digits are $3$ and $2$.
4. $(c)$: $400 \div 20 = 20$, so the missing digit is $2$.
5. $(d)$: the dividend $100\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$ must be a multiple of $50$. Only $1000$ works, and $1000 \div 50 = 20$, so the missing digits are $0$ and $2$.
6. $(e)$: only the divisor $4$ fits. $848 \div 4 = 212$ (digits $4$ and $2$) or $868 \div 4 = 217$ (digits $6$ and $7$).
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution]
7. $(f)$: the dividend is $936$, and $936 \div 3 = 312$, so the missing digits are $9$, $1$ and $2$.
8. $(g)$: $88$ can be divided exactly by $1$, $2$, $4$ or $8$: the quotient is $88$, $44$, $22$ or $11$.
9. $(h)$: there are many answers, for example $950 \div 5 = 190$, $920 \div 2 = 460$, $930 \div 3 = 310$ and $990 \div 9 = 110$.
10. (i): a quotient with $3$ digits needs the divisor $1$, and $180 \div 1 = 180$.
11. $(j)$: $6,480 \div 8 = 810$ and $6,480 \div 9 = 720$ both fit.
12. Check by multiplying back, for example $4 \times 120 = 480$ and $8 \times 810 = 6,480$.
Answer: $(a)$: $120$; $(b)$: $302$; $(c)$: $20$; $(d)$: $20$; $(e)$: $212$ or $217$; $(f)$: $312$; $(g)$: $88$, $44$, $22$ or $11$; $(h)$: many; (i): $180$; $(j)$: $810$ or $720$
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution (continued)]

content.text:
1. Predict first: 94 coconuts are packed in bags of 8. Do you need 11 bags or 12 bags? And what if the 94 coconuts are shared among 8 customers?
2. 94 ÷ 8: quotient 11, remainder 6, because 94 = 8 × 11 + 6.
3. Packing in bags: 11 full bags hold 88 coconuts. The 6 coconuts left still need a bag, so 11 + 1 = 12 bags.
4. Sharing among customers: each customer gets 11 coconuts. The 6 left over are not shared, so the answer is 11 each.
5. Always read the story: when the leftover needs a container, add one more. When it is not shared, the quotient is the answer.
6. Rule: the same remainder can mean one more bag or a few left over, depending on the story.

content.text:
Worked example: 94 coconuts (practice values). How many bags of 8 are needed? If the 94 coconuts are shared equally among 8 customers, how many does each get?
1. Take away 10 groups of 8: 8 × 10 = 80, and 94 − 80 = 14.
2. Take away 1 group of 8: 8 × 1 = 8, and 14 − 8 = 6.
3. Add the groups taken away: 10 + 1 = 11.
4. 6 is left. It is less than 8, so no more groups of 8 can be taken away.
5. So 94 ÷ 8: quotient 11, remainder 6.
6. Check: 94 = 8 × 11 + 6.
7. Bags: the 11 full bags hold 88 coconuts and 6 are left. The 6 need one more bag, so 11 + 1 = 12 bags.
8. Sharing: each of the 8 customers gets 11 coconuts, and the 6 left over are not shared.
Answer: 12 bags are needed, and each customer gets 11 coconuts

content.text:
1. Predict first: onions cost ₹18 for 1 kg and 45 kg were sold. How much money is that? And if the bill says ₹990, how many kg were sold?
2. A bill has three numbers: the cost of 1 kg, the quantity in kg, and the total amount. Total amount = cost of 1 kg × quantity.
3. Total: 18 × 45 = 810, so 45 kg of onions cost ₹810.
4. Missing quantity: the total is ₹990 and 1 kg costs ₹18, so the quantity is 990 ÷ 18 = 55 kg. Check: 18 × 55 = 990.
5. Missing cost: the total is ₹1260 for 36 kg, so 1 kg costs 1260 ÷ 36 = ₹35. Check: 35 × 36 = 1260.
6. Look at a real bill from a shop and name the information it records. Which number could you find by dividing?
7. Rule: if the total is missing, multiply. If the quantity or the cost of 1 kg is missing, divide the total by the number you know.

Worked example: A bill has onions at ₹18 for 1 kg and 45 kg sold (practice values). Find the total. Then find the quantity for a total of ₹990, and the cost of 1 kg for 36 kg with a total of ₹1260.
1. Total amount = cost of 1 kg × quantity.
2. Total: 18 × 45 = 810, so the total is ₹810.
3. Check 18 × 45: 18 × 40 = 720 and 18 × 5 = 90, and 720 + 90 = 810.
4. Missing quantity: 990 ÷ 18 = 55 kg, because 18 × 55 = 990.
5. Missing cost: 1260 ÷ 36 = 35, because 35 × 36 = 1260, so 1 kg costs ₹35.
Answer: The total is ₹810, the quantity is 55 kg and 1 kg costs ₹35

content.book_number: Let Us Solve (word problems): Rani's samosas
content.question: Rani is planning to host a party. She estimates that 250 guests will attend. She plans to serve one samosa to each guest. Samosas are available in packs of 6 or 8. Which pack should Rani buy? Explain your answer.
steps: Rani needs 250 samosas, one for each guest.
Packs of 6: 250 ÷ 6: quotient 41, remainder 4, because 250 = 6 × 41 + 4. The 4 left need one more pack, so 41 + 1 = 42 packs.
42 packs of 6 are 42 × 6 = 252 samosas, which is 252 − 250 = 2 extra.
Packs of 8: 250 ÷ 8: quotient 31, remainder 2, because 250 = 8 × 31 + 2. The 2 left need one more pack, so 31 + 1 = 32 packs.
32 packs of 8 are 32 × 8 = 256 samosas, which is 256 − 250 = 6 extra.
Packs of 6 leave 2 extra samosas and packs of 8 leave 6 extra, so packs of 6 waste fewer.
The book gives no prices, so this is the plan's reading: the pack with fewer extra samosas.
content.answer: Sample answer: packs of 6, 42 packs with 2 extra (packs of 8: 32 packs with 6 extra). Your answer may differ

content.text: Find the solutions for part A. Observe the relations between the quotient, divisor and dividend and use it to answer parts B and C.

content.text:
1. Predict first: 480 ÷ 12 = 40. If you double 480 and still divide by 12, will the answer be double, half or the same?
2. Think of a rectangle. Its area is the dividend N, one side is the divisor D and the other side is the quotient Q, so N = D × Q.
3. Double the dividend: 960 ÷ 12 = 80. The area doubled and one side stayed, so the other side, the quotient, doubled.
4. Double the divisor: 480 ÷ 24 = 20. The area stayed and one side doubled, so the other side, the quotient, is halved.
5. Double both: 960 ÷ 24 = 40. The area doubled and one side doubled, so the quotient stays the same.
6. Rule: double the dividend and the quotient doubles. Double the divisor and the quotient halves. Double both and the quotient is the same.

tool_config.screen: A notice board on the wall of the packing shed on Susie and Sunitha's coconut farm, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A plot of coconut trees drawn as a rectangle is the largest thing on screen: its area is the dividend N, one side is the divisor D and the other side is the quotient Q, each labelled with its number. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Four buttons sit under the rectangle: Double the dividend, Halve the dividend, Double the divisor and Halve the divisor. Each press redraws the rectangle and shows the new division. A prediction card asks if the quotient will be more, less or the same, and a related list on the right stores each new division. Controls: tap a change button; tap more, less or the same; type the new quotient; Check, Hint, Retry (restores the start rectangle of this card), Reset (clears the related list), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the dividend, the divisor, the quotient and the area line N = D × Q, and a card number out of 7.

2. $(b)$: $704 \div 22$: $704$ is double $352$ and $22$ is double $11$, so the quotient is the same: $704 \div 22 = 32$.
3. $(c)$: $704 \div 11$: the dividend is doubled and the divisor is the same, so the quotient doubles: $704 \div 11 = 64$.
4. $(d)$: $352 \div 22$: the divisor is doubled and the dividend is the same, so the quotient is halved: $352 \div 22 = 16$.
[Image: Let Us Solve (relations): Ans3: solution]

6. Check: $22 \times 32 = 704$, $11 \times 64 = 704$, $22 \times 16 = 352$ and $44 \times 32 = 1,408$.
Answer: $(a)$: $32$; $(b)$: $32$; $(c)$: $64$; $(d)$: $16$; $(e)$: $32$

content.text:
1. Predict first: is 6 × 5 = 20 + 10 true or false? Find the value of each side before you decide.
2. A statement with an equal sign is true when both sides have the same value.
3. 6 × 5 = 30 and 20 + 10 = 30. Both sides are 30, so the statement is true.
4. Now compare 18 ÷ 3 with 2 × 4. The first is 6 and the second is 8. They are different, so a statement that says they are equal is false.
5. To complete 9 × 4 = ___ + 16: the left side is 36, so the blank must be 36 − 16 = 20. Check: 20 + 16 = 36.
6. The equal sign does not mean that the answer comes next. It means both sides have the same value.
7. Rule: find the value of both sides. The same value is true, different values is false.

content.text:
Worked example: Decide if the statement that 6 × 5 equals 20 + 10 is true or false, and the same for the statement that 18 ÷ 3 equals 2 × 4, and complete 9 × 4 = ___ + 16 (practice values).
1. 6 × 5 = 30 and 20 + 10 = 30. The two sides have the same value, so the first statement is true.
2. 18 ÷ 3 = 6 and 2 × 4 = 8. The two sides are different, so the second statement is false.
3. For the third statement the left side is 9 × 4 = 36.
4. The blank must make the right side 36 too, so the blank is 36 − 16 = 20.
5. Check: 20 + 16 = 36, which is the left side.
Answer: The first is true, the second is false, and the blank is 20

tool_config.title: Equal Balance
tool_config.idea: Find the value of both sides of an equal sign on a balance to decide if a statement is true, and complete a statement by making both sides the same.
tool_config.screen: The market scale at the stall on Susie and Sunitha's coconut farm, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A balance with a left pan and a right pan is the largest thing on screen. Number and operation cards make a side, for example 3 × 8 on one pan and 20 + 4 on the other, and a value read-out sits above each pan. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. When the two values are equal the beam is level and glows green, when they differ the beam tips toward the bigger side. A blank slot on one side holds a missing number. Under the balance are two tags, True and False. Controls: drag cards to the pans; type a number into the blank slot; tap True or False; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the pans), Reset (restores the starting card), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the value of each side, whether the beam is level, and a card number out of 7.
student_does: The balance shows 6 × 5 on the left and 20 + 10 on the right, level (practice values). Find the value of each side. Then press Next.
Put a statement on the balance, find the value of both sides, decide if it is true or false, and complete a statement by typing the missing number.
Decide if the book's five statements are true or false, and complete the book's four statements so that they are true.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): 3 × 8 and 20 + 4. Answer: both sides are 24, the beam is level, so the statement is true.
Card 2 (practice values): 40 − 9 and 5 × 7. Answer: the left side is 31 and the right side is 35, the beam tips to the right, so the statement is false.
Card 3 (practice values): 56 ÷ 7 and 4 × 2. Answer: both sides are 8, so the statement is true.
Card 4 (practice values): complete 9 × 4 = ___ + 16. Answer: the left side is 36, so the blank is 36 − 16 = 20. Check: 20 + 16 = 36.
Card 5 (practice values): complete ___ ÷ 6 = 18 ÷ 3. Answer: the right side is 6, so the blank divided by 6 must be 6, and the blank is 6 × 6 = 36.

Challenge: 'Find out whether the following statements are True (T) or False (F). A true sentence is one where both sides of the = sign have the same value.' The five statements put these on the left and right of the equal sign: (a) 8 × 9 and 70 + 2, (b) 20 − 6 and 7 × 3, (c) 48 ÷ 3 and 4 × 4, (d) 89 − 9 and 90 + 0, (e) 25 + 10 and 45 − 10. Answer: (a) T, (b) F, (c) T, (d) F, (e) T.

Challenge: 'Complete the following statements such that they are true.' (a) 7 × 6 equals a blank plus 17, (b) 87 + 6 equals a blank times 31, (c) 63 plus a blank equals 74 − 4, (d) a blank divided by 9 equals 16 ÷ 2. Answer: (a) 25, (b) 3, (c) 7, (d) 72. Next stop: always, sometimes or never true.
feedback: When the values are equal the beam levels and the tool says, for example: Both sides are 24, so the statement is true.
When the values differ the beam tips and the tool says, for example: The left side is 31 and the right side is 35, so the statement is false.
A blank filled with a wrong number tips the beam and says: The two sides are not the same yet. What number makes this side 36?
A card dropped on the wrong pan slides back with a clue such as: Which side does this card belong to?
Each side shows its value as soon as its cards are in place, so the student always sees what is being compared.
tool_config.done_when: The student has found the value of both sides for every card, decided if each statement is true or false, and completed the book's four statements.

hint_ladder.text: Look at the statement. What are the two sides of the equal sign?
Find the value of the left side, then find the value of the right side.
If both values are the same, the statement is true. If a number is missing, make the side with the blank have the same value as the other side.
For 9 × 4 = ___ + 16: the left side is 36, so the blank is 36 − 16 = 20.

(e): 25 + 10 = 35 and 45 − 10 = 35. The same value, so True.

steps: Find the side that has no blank, then make the other side the same.
(a): the left side 7 × 6 is 42, so the blank is 42 − 17 = 25. Check: 25 + 17 = 42.
(b): the left side 87 + 6 is 93, so the blank is 93 ÷ 31 = 3. Check: 3 × 31 = 93.
(c): the right side 74 − 4 is 70, so the blank is 70 − 63 = 7. Check: 63 + 7 = 70.
(d): the right side 16 ÷ 2 is 8, so the blank is 8 × 9 = 72. Check: 72 ÷ 9 = 8.

content.text:
1. Predict first: is "Adding 2 to an even number gives an even number" always, sometimes or never true? Test it with some numbers.
2. Test with examples: 4 + 2 = 6, 10 + 2 = 12 and 16 + 2 = 18. All are even. No example fails, so it is always true.
3. Test "Adding 1 to an even number gives an even number": 4 + 1 = 5 and 10 + 1 = 11 are odd. No example works, so it is never true.
4. Test "Multiplying a number by 3 gives an even number": 3 × 4 = 12 is even, but 3 × 5 = 15 is odd. Some work and some fail, so it is sometimes true.
5. One example that fails shows a statement is not always true. One example that works shows it is not never true.
6. Many examples that work do not prove a statement is always true. Look for an example that fails.
7. Rule: always true means no example fails, never true means no example works, sometimes true means some work and some fail.

Worked example: Decide if each statement is always, sometimes or never true (practice values): adding 2 to an even number gives an even number; adding 1 to an even number gives an even number; multiplying a number by 3 gives an even number.

3. Statement 3: 3 × 4 = 12 is even, and 3 × 5 = 15 is odd. One works and one fails, so it is sometimes true.
4. One example that fails is enough to show a statement is not always true.
Answer: The first is always true, the second is never true, and the third is sometimes true

tool_config.title: Always, Sometimes, Never
tool_config.idea: Test a statement with number examples and decide if it is always true, sometimes true or never true, knowing that one example that fails shows it is not always true.
tool_config.screen: Three baskets on the market stall at Susie and Sunitha's coconut farm, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The baskets are labelled Always true, Sometimes true and Never true and are the largest things on screen. A statement card sits above them. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. A tray of number cards, from 1 to 20, lets the student pick a number to test, and a result strip shows each test as works or does not work, with the sum or product worked out. Controls: tap a number card to test it; drag the statement card into a basket; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the tests of this card), Reset (restores the statement), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the numbers tested, how many work and how many fail, and a card number out of 7.
student_does: The statement is 'Adding 4 to an even number gives an even number' (practice values). Test it with three numbers and say what you see. Then press Next.
Test each statement with several numbers, watch the works and does not work count, and drop the statement into the right basket.
Test the book's three statements and give the examples the book asks for, then place the book's five statements in the right baskets.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): 'Adding 2 to an even number gives an even number.' Answer: 4 + 2 = 6, 10 + 2 = 12 and 16 + 2 = 18 are all even, none fails, so it is always true.
Card 2 (practice values): 'Adding 1 to an even number gives an even number.' Answer: 4 + 1 = 5 and 10 + 1 = 11 are odd, none works, so it is never true.
Card 3 (practice values): 'Multiplying a number by 3 gives an even number.' Answer: 3 × 4 = 12 is even and 3 × 5 = 15 is odd, some work and some fail, so it is sometimes true.
Card 4 (practice values): 'Doubling a number gives an even number.' Answer: 2 × 3 = 6, 2 × 7 = 14 and 2 × 10 = 20 are all even, none fails, so it is always true.
Card 5 (practice values): 'Adding 3 to an odd number gives an even number.' Answer: 5 + 3 = 8, 7 + 3 = 10 and 9 + 3 = 12 are all even, none fails, so it is always true.

Challenge: 'Think about the following statements and find examples as suggested below.' (a) 'When two odd numbers are added, the sum is even.' Find 5 examples. Can you find an example to show it can be false? (b) 'Multiplying a number by 2 can give an odd number.' Give some examples. Can you find any? (c) 'Halving a number always leads to an even number.' Give 3 examples. Can you find 3 examples when this is not true? Answer: (a) always true, for example 1 + 3 = 4 and 9 + 9 = 18, no example is false; (b) never true, 2 × 3 = 6 and 2 × 5 = 10 are even; (c) sometimes true, half of 8 is 4 but half of 6 is 3.

Challenge: 'Tick in the appropriate cell for the following statements.' (a) Adding 10 to a number gives a multiple of ten. (b) Changing the order of the numbers in subtraction makes no difference. (c) In multiplication, doubling one number and halving the other keeps the product the same. (d) Multiplication by an odd number gives an even number. (e) Multiplying a number by 5 leads to numbers which have 0 in the Ones place. Answer: (a) sometimes, (b) sometimes, only for two equal numbers, (c) always, (d) sometimes, (e) sometimes. Next stop: the revision of the chapter.
feedback: Each tested number is added to the result strip with its working, for example: 6 is even and 6 + 2 = 8 is even, it works.
When a number fails the tool says: This one does not work. One example that fails is enough to show the statement is not always true.
When all the tests work the tool asks: Can you find a number that fails? Try an odd number or a big number.
A statement dropped in the wrong basket slides back with a clue such as: Did every number you tested work?
The works and fail counts update after each test, so the student sees which basket fits.
tool_config.done_when: The student has tested every statement with several numbers, sorted the statements of the cards and the book into the right baskets, and given the examples the book asks for.

It works this example: Decide if each statement is always, sometimes or never true (practice values): adding 2 to an even number gives an even number; adding 1 to an even number gives an even number; multiplying a number by 3 gives an even number.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: is "Adding 2 to an even number gives an even number" always, sometimes or never true? Test it with some numbers. Test with examples: 4 + 2 = 6, 10 + 2 = 12 and 16 + 2 = 18. All are even. No example fails, so it is always true. Test "Adding 1 to an even number gives an even number": 4 + 1 = 5 and 10 + 1 = 11 are odd. No example works, so it is never true. Test "Multiplying a number by 3 gives an even number": 3 × 4 = 12 is even, but 3 × 5 = 15 is odd. Some work and some fail, so it is sometimes true. One example that fails shows a statement is not always true. One example that works shows it is not never true. Many examples that work do not prove a statement is always true. Look for an example that fails. Rule: always true means no example fails, never true means no example works, sometimes true means some work and some fail. 1. Statement 1: test 4 + 2 = 6, 10 + 2 = 12 and 16 + 2 = 18. All are even and none fails, so it is always true. 2. Statement 2: test 4 + 1 = 5 and 10 + 1 = 11. Both are odd and none works, so it is never true. 3. Statement 3: 3 × 4 = 12 is even, and 3 × 5 = 15 is odd. One works and one fails, so it is sometimes true. 4. One example that fails is enough to show a statement is not always true. Answer: The first is always true, the second is never true, and the third is sometimes true

content.question: Think about the following statements and find examples as suggested below. (a): “When two odd numbers are added, the sum is even.” Find 5 examples for the above statement. Can you find an example to show that the statement can be false?
steps: The statement: when two odd numbers are added, the sum is even.
Five examples: 1 + 3 = 4, 3 + 5 = 8, 7 + 9 = 16, 5 + 11 = 16 and 9 + 9 = 18. All the sums are even.
Try more: 11 + 13 = 24 and 15 + 1 = 16. These sums are even too.
Why: each odd number has one left over when counted in pairs, and the two left overs make one more pair, so the sum has none left over.
No example shows the statement false, so it is always true.
